To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) socioeconomic inequalities in health were observed for all maternal and child health outcomes; (2) socioeconomic gradients were more pronounced for individual socioeconomic position (education and income) than for neighborhood socioeconomic position and combined socioeconomic position; and (3) there was no consistent gradient for combined socioeconomic position, but the category with low individual socioeconomic position and high neighborhood socioeconomic position often had the poorest health outcomes.

socioeconomic disparities in maternal and child health outcomes in Canada are consistent across a wide range of outcomes, with the strongest associations found for maternal health outcomes, and that these associations are stronger for individual socioeconomic position than for neighbourhood socioeconomic position.
socioeconomic disparities are consistent and large for most maternal and child health outcomes, and that the magnitude and direction of these disparities are different across the outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of patterns in health inequalities across multiple MCH outcomes.
the identification and measurement of health inequalities in the context of the social determinants of health (SDOH).

the identification of the patterns of social inequalities across a range of pregnancy and birth outcomes, and the examination of the consistency of these patterns and their magnitudes across the outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are large and consistent socioeconomic disparities in multiple MCH indicators that can be addressed by policies and interventions at the individual and community levels.
there are consistent socioeconomic inequalities for multiple maternal and infant health outcomes in Canada, with some variation by SEP measures.
there are consistent socioeconomic disparities in maternal and child health across multiple outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most disadvantaged women have the poorest MCH outcomes and that these outcomes are often associated with a combination of poor individual and neighborhood SEP.
SEP inequalities exist in all MCH outcomes but they vary by the type of SEP measure and by the MCH outcomes.
the more complex the health care need, the more likely it is that the SEP gradient is weak or non-existent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple health outcomes that are important and that are affected by social inequalities.
SEP inequalities exist in multiple health care needs and these inequalities are large and persistent.
the health of pregnant women, infants and families is affected by multiple factors that operate at individual and population levels, which should be considered in policy and research.
